title: Question 1.1
statement_text: Given a graph $\Gamma$, can we decompose it as the joined union of smaller graphs?
context_text: Graphs are finite, simple and undirected. A homogeneous set (module) of a graph $\Gamma$ is a set $X$ of vertices such that every vertex outside $X$ is adjacent to all or to none of the vertices of $X$; it is non-trivial if $2\le|X|<|V(\Gamma)|$, and $\Gamma$ is prime if it has no non-trivial homogeneous set. For a graph $G$ on vertices $v_1,\dots,v_d$ and graphs $G_1,\dots,G_d$, the joined union $G[G_1,\dots,G_d]$ is obtained from the disjoint union of $G_1,\dots,G_d$ by joining every vertex of $G_i$ to every vertex of $G_j$ whenever $v_iv_j$ is an edge of $G$ (the wreath or lexicographic product is the case where all $G_i$ are equal). Each $G_i$ is a homogeneous set of $G[G_1,\dots,G_d]$, and conversely a graph has a non-trivial homogeneous set iff it can be written as such a joined union with some $G_i$ having more than one vertex, so the question amounts to deciding whether $\Gamma$ is prime; this is classically studied through modular decomposition, and homogeneous sets can be found in polynomial time. The question is motivated by the study of phase oscillators on multilayer networks, where a joined-union decomposition lets solutions of a reduced system be broadcast to the full network. The paper answers it for Cayley graphs: if $S\ne\emptyset$ and $S\ne G\setminus\{1\}$, then $\mathrm{Cay}(G,S)$ has a non-trivial homogeneous set iff $G$ has a non-trivial subgroup $H$ such that $Hc\subseteq S$ for every $c\in S\setminus H$; moreover a vertex-transitive graph that is neither complete nor edgeless is a non-trivial wreath product iff it is not prime.
notes: The paper answers this question in the special case of Cayley graphs; the general question for arbitrary graphs is classical and studied via modular decomposition theory.

title: Question 4.28
statement_text: For a finite commutative ring $R$, when is the unitary Cayley graph $X_R=\mathrm{Cay}((R,+),R^{\times})$ prime?
context_text: Graphs are finite, simple and undirected. A homogeneous set (module) of a graph $\Gamma$ is a set $X$ of vertices such that every vertex outside $X$ is adjacent to all or to none of the vertices of $X$; it is non-trivial if $2\le|X|<|V(\Gamma)|$, and $\Gamma$ is prime if it has no non-trivial homogeneous set. For a finite commutative ring $R$ with group of units $R^\times$, the unitary Cayley graph $X_R=\mathrm{Cay}((R,+),R^\times)$ has vertex set $R$, with $x$ and $y$ adjacent iff $y-x$ is a unit. For a subgroup $S$ of $R^\times$ with $-1\in S$, the authors show that if $\mathrm{Cay}(R,S)$ is connected and its complement is connected, then it is prime iff the pair $(R,S)$ has no non-trivial quotient, and a non-prime such graph has a non-trivial ideal that is a homogeneous set. For $X_R$, since $X_{R_1\times R_2}\cong X_{R_1}\times X_{R_2}$ (tensor product) and units are detected modulo the Jacobson radical, $X_R$ is not prime unless $R$ is semisimple, i.e. a product of finite fields $k_1\times\dots\times k_d$, in which case $X_R\cong\prod_iK_{|k_i|}$. The paper answers the question completely: $X_R$ is prime iff $R=\mathbb{F}_2$, or $R\cong\prod_{i=1}^dk_i$ with $d\ge2$ fields $k_i$ at most one of which has size $2$.
notes: This question appears to be answered within the paper via Theorem 4.35; it is posed as the key structural question leading to the main results.

title: Question 4.31
statement_text: Let $n_{1},\ldots,n_{d}$ be positive integers. When is $\prod_{i=1}^{d}K_{n_{i}}$ prime?
context_text: Graphs are finite, simple and undirected. A homogeneous set (module) of a graph $\Gamma$ is a set $X$ of vertices such that every vertex outside $X$ is adjacent to all or to none of the vertices of $X$; it is non-trivial if $2\le|X|<|V(\Gamma)|$, and $\Gamma$ is prime if it has no non-trivial homogeneous set. The tensor (direct, Kronecker) product $\prod_{i=1}^dK_{n_i}$ has as vertices the $d$-tuples $(s_1,\dots,s_d)$ with $0\le s_i\le n_i-1$, two tuples being adjacent iff they differ in every coordinate. The question arises from unitary Cayley graphs: for a finite commutative ring $R$, $X_R=\mathrm{Cay}((R,+),R^\times)$ (adjacency when the difference is a unit) is prime only if $R$ is a product of finite fields $k_1\times\dots\times k_d$, and then $X_R\cong\prod_iK_{|k_i|}$, so primeness of $X_R$ reduces to this question with $n_i=|k_i|$. For $d=1$, $K_n$ is not prime unless $n\le2$. For $d\ge2$ the complement of the product is connected, and the authors show the product is connected iff at most one $n_i$ equals $2$. When every $n_i$ is the size of a finite field, they conclude that the product is prime iff it is connected, i.e. iff at most one $n_i=2$. The paper does not explicitly treat general $n_i$ (for instance $n_i=6$), for which the ring-theoretic argument does not directly apply.
notes: This question is addressed by Theorem 4.35 within the paper; it is the combinatorial core to which the algebraic problem of Question 4.28 is reduced.
